introduction: This foundational level introduces the agrarian legal framework of India. Since 'Land' and 'Land Revenue' are State subjects under List II of the Constitution, every state has its own Code (e.g., UP Revenue Code 2006, MP Land Revenue Code 1959). These codes govern who owns agricultural land, how revenue is collected, and how disputes are settled outside of regular civil courts.

core_concepts.title: The Revenue Court Hierarchy
core_concepts.description:
Unlike regular Civil Courts (District Judge -> Munsif), land disputes are handled by a parallel executive-judicial hierarchy to ensure speedy disposal by officers who understand agrarian ground realities.
1. Board of Revenue (The Apex Revenue Court in the State).
2. Commissioner / Additional Commissioner (Divisional level).
3. Collector / District Magistrate (District level).
4. Sub-Divisional Officer (SDO / SDM).
5. Tahsildar & Naib-Tahsildar.
6. Revenue Inspector & Lekhpal/Patwari (Field officers, not courts).

core_concepts.title: Record of Rights (Khatauni) & Khasra
core_concepts.description:
The foundation of agrarian administration is meticulous record-keeping.
- Khasra: The primary field book. It is a plot-wise record containing details of the soil, the crops grown, and irrigation sources for a specific plot of land.
- Khatauni (Record of Rights): The definitive register of persons holding land. It lists the name of the tenure-holder (farmer), the class of tenancy, and the total land revenue payable by them.

core_concepts.title: Mutation (Dakhil Kharij)
core_concepts.description:
Meaning 'Entry and Deletion'.
- The Rule: Whenever agricultural land changes hands—either through succession (death of the father) or transfer (sale/gift)—the new owner MUST report it to the Tahsildar. The Tahsildar deletes the old owner's name from the Khatauni and enters the new owner's name.
- Purpose: It ensures the State knows exactly who is liable to pay the land revenue going forward.

core_concepts.title: Bar on Civil Court Jurisdiction
core_concepts.description:
A core principle across all state codes (e.g., Sec 206 UP Code, Sec 257 MPLRC). 
- The Rule: Regular Civil Courts are strictly barred from taking cognizance of any suit or application regarding matters that a Revenue Court is empowered to decide (e.g., assessing land revenue, partition of agricultural holdings, or declaring tenancy rights).

important_entities.name: Mutation DOES NOT Confer Title
important_entities.key_fact: A highly tested Supreme Court doctrine.
important_entities.significance: The Supreme Court has repeatedly ruled (*Smt. Sawarni v. Smt. Inder Kaur*) that mutation of a property in revenue records neither creates nor extinguishes title (ownership) to the property. Mutation is purely for 'fiscal purposes' (collecting tax). If A's name is wrongfully mutated, B can still file a title suit in a competent court to prove true ownership.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will ask: 'Does the Land Revenue Code apply to a commercial shopping mall built in the center of the city?' **NO**. Land Revenue Codes generally apply only to agricultural land, grove land, or rural *Abadi* (village habitation) land. Once agricultural land is officially 'diverted' or declared as non-agricultural/urban area under the Code, it falls under municipal/urban laws, not the Revenue Code.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: B C C S T (Board, Commissioner, Collector, SDO, Tahsildar)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Memorize the strict top-down appellate hierarchy of revenue courts.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary Prelims question asks 'Which document is known as the Record of Rights in agrarian law?', unconditionally select **Khatauni** [1.1.3].
